```markdown
# Batch tracking design

Date: 2026-10-28
Status: Agreed in conversation. Build choices in section 5 were made without discussion and are open to review.

## 1. Goal

Trace any bottle back to the ingredients that went into it.

The trace chain is:

bottle label → batch → every sack lot used in that batch

## 2. Scope

In scope:

- Record a batch from mash day to bottling.
- Record the lot number of each malt and hop sack when a brewer opens it for a batch.
- Print the batch number and the bottling date on each bottle label.
- Look up a batch and show all of its sack lots.

Out of scope:

- Inventory and stock levels.
- Recipes and brewing process data, such as temperatures and gravity readings.
- Tracking of single bottles. The label identifies the batch, not the bottle.

## 3. Agreed behavior

### 3.1 Batch

A batch is one brew. It starts on mash day and ends at bottling. Each batch has a unique batch number.

### 3.2 Sack lots

Each malt and hop sack has a lot number from the supplier. When a brewer opens a sack for a batch, the brewer scans the lot number. Brewers do not type lot numbers, because their hands are usually wet.

One sack can supply more than one batch. One batch uses many sacks.

### 3.3 Bottling run

At bottling, the label printer prints the batch number and the bottling date on each label.

### 3.4 Trace

A user enters a batch number from a bottle label. The app shows the batch and the lot number of each sack that went into it.

## 4. Fit with the existing app

The feature goes into the existing Flask app on the office Raspberry Pi. It uses the same SQLite database as the taproom tabs. It adds no new server and no new service.

## 5. Build choices (not discussed, open to review)

### 5.1 Data model

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `batches` | `batch_number` (unique), `mash_date`, `bottling_date` (empty until bottled), `notes` |
| `lots` | `lot_number`, `ingredient` (for example, "Maris Otter" or "Cascade"), `supplier` |
| `batch_lots` | One row for each sack opened for a batch: `batch_id`, `lot_id`, `opened_at` |

`batch_lots` is a link table. It records the many-to-many link between batches and lots. With this table, the trace also works in the reverse direction: from a lot number to every batch that used it. This direction matters if a supplier recalls a lot.

A lot is created the first time a brewer scans it. A brewer can add the ingredient name and supplier at that time or later.

### 5.2 Scanning

The design assumes that each sack shows its lot number as a barcode.

Use a USB barcode scanner in keyboard mode. In this mode, the scanner sends the scanned text as key presses, then Enter. A normal web form field receives the scan. The app needs no scanner driver.

The scan screen has one large input field for the current batch. Each scan adds one row to `batch_lots`. The screen shows the last scan in large text, so a brewer can confirm it from a distance.

If a sack has no barcode, a brewer can type the lot number. This is a fallback only.

### 5.3 Label printing

The design does not yet know the label printer model or how it connects. The app shows the batch number and the bottling date in a form that the current label workflow can use. Direct control of the printer is a later step, after we know the model.

### 5.4 Trace screen

One search field accepts a batch number or a lot number.

- A batch number shows the batch dates and all lots.
- A lot number shows all batches that used the lot.

## 6. Risks

- **One copy of the data.** The trace records live only on the Pi's SD card. SD cards fail. A nightly copy of the SQLite file to another machine reduces this risk.
- **Missed scans.** If a brewer forgets to scan a sack, the trace has a gap. The batch screen shows the lot count, so a brewer can check it before bottling.
- **Duplicate scans.** A brewer can scan the same sack twice. The app warns on a duplicate scan for the same batch, but it does not block the scan.

## 7. Next step

Write an implementation plan from this design.
```

The design is written up at `docs/plans/2026-10-28-batch-tracking-design.md`.

Sections 2 to 4 record what you agreed to. You can skip them.

Section 5 is different. We did not discuss how to build the feature, so I made those choices myself. Please skim section 5 before we build. These assumptions are the most likely to be wrong:

- **Barcodes on the sacks.** I assumed that the lot numbers on the sacks are printed as barcodes. If they are text only, the scan design must change.
- **The label printer.** I do not know the printer model. The design leaves direct printer control for later.
- **Reverse trace.** I added a lookup from a lot number to its batches. The schema supports it at no extra cost, and it helps if a supplier recalls a lot.

If section 5 looks right, the next step is an implementation plan. I suggest that you run the build from that plan in a fresh Sonnet session (`claude --model sonnet`).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The `batch_lots` link table carries the design. One sack feeds several batches and one batch uses many sacks, so neither `batches` nor `lots` can hold the link alone. The table also gives the reverse trace (lot → batches) with no extra work.
- A USB scanner in keyboard mode suits a Flask app. It "types" the barcode and presses Enter, so a plain HTML form receives the scan. This keeps the Pi free of drivers.
- The trace data shares one SQLite file on one SD card with the taproom tabs. The tabs are only a convenience. The trace data is a record you may need years later, so backup is listed as a risk.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
